title: Attribute Latency With Traces, Not Averages
objective: Instrument one request path with a parent span and at least three child spans, capture a fast and a slow trace, and explain where wall time went — including any disagreement with the CPU profile from pe1t1-002.
whyThisMatters: CPU profiles explain burn. They do not explain waiting. A p95 that is 'slow' because of I/O, locks, or a downstream call will not show up as the hottest CPU frame. Traces are how you attribute wall-clock latency to a span you can name.
evidence: Instrumentation that creates one parent span and at least three named child spans on a single request path
A fast-request trace export (JSON, OTLP dump, or equivalent) with each span duration in milliseconds
A slow-request trace export for the same operation, similarly timed
A comparison note stating the largest child span's share of the slow request as a computed percentage, and whether that span matches the hottest CPU frame from pe1t1-002
Reflection notes answering the task questions
acceptanceCriteria: A captured trace for one request includes a parent span and at least three distinctly named child spans.
Fast and slow traces for the same operation are both committed, each listing span durations in milliseconds.
The comparison note computes the largest child span's share of the slow parent duration as a percentage from those milliseconds.
The note states match or mismatch with the hottest CPU frame from pe1t1-002 (or a re-taken profile in this task) and names the difference if they disagree.
